title: ArrayList expansion: threshold, default size 10, grows ~50%
keyPoints: Expansion is triggered when size equals capacity and a new element is added
The formula is newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), which gives approximately 1.5x growth
Growth sequence from default: 10 to 15 to 22 to 33 to 49 to 73 to 109 to 163
Each expansion allocates a new array and copies all existing elements via Arrays.copyOf()
The add operation is amortized O(1) because each element is copied O(log n) times across all resizes
Pre-allocate with new ArrayList<>(n) to avoid the O(n) copy cost of repeated expansions
ensureCapacity(n) pre-grows the array before a batch of additions to avoid multiple small resizes

s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayList expands when size equals capacity: it creates a new array at 1.5x the old capacity and copies all elements, giving amortized O(1) add performance.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Trigger**: expansion happens when `size == elementData.length` and you call `add()`
- **Formula**: `newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` – approximately 50% growth (1.5x)
- **Mechanism**: `Arrays.copyOf(elementData, newCapacity)` allocates a new array and copies all elements using native `System.arraycopy()`
- **Amortized O(1)**: although each resize is O(n), resizes happen infrequently enough that the average cost per add is O(1)
- **Pre-allocation**: `new ArrayList<>(n)` or `ensureCapacity(n)` avoids repeated resizing when the expected size is known
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a bank branch that starts with a 10-seat waiting area. When all 10 seats are full and a new customer arrives, the branch builds a bigger room with 15 seats (1.5x), moves all 10 customers to the new room, and seats customer 11. The old room is demolished. When the 15-seat room fills up, they build a 22-seat room, and so on. If the branch knows it will serve 1000 customers today, it builds a 1000-seat room from the start.

sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayList expansion is triggered when the internal array is full and a new element arrives. The growth formula `newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)` gives approximately 1.5x growth, which balances speed against memory waste. Each expansion allocates a new array and copies all elements using the native `System.arraycopy()` method.

The key insight is amortized analysis. Although each resize costs O(n), resizes happen exponentially less frequently. Over n additions, the total copy count is about 3n, making the average cost per add O(1). This is the same principle as the banker's method in algorithm analysis: each element pays a small constant upfront to cover future copy costs.

In the National Bank of India's end-of-day batch processing, Rajesh loads 2 million transaction records. Without pre-allocation, the ArrayList resizes about 40 times, creating 40 garbage arrays and copying tens of millions of element references. With `new ArrayList<>(2_000_000)`, there is one allocation and zero resizes. After loading, `trimToSize()` reclaims any unused capacity.

Remember one sentence: ArrayList grows by 1.5x when full, which gives amortized O(1) adds, but pre-allocate with the constructor when you know the expected size.
